transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in today?

Hi, doctor. Yeah, um… what finally pushed me to come in is I just can’t seem to organize all the moving parts anymore. It’s like I’ve got patent notes over here, workshop prep, gallery deadlines, team decisions… and somehow I end up doing whatever is loudest in the moment instead of what actually matters.

And I mean, I’m a software developer, so you’d think I’d be good at systems, right? I can structure code, but my own stuff just turns into this pile of half-sorted priorities. It’s been getting hard to keep up.
Outside of work, do you also find it hard to stay organized or focused—like with personal tasks, relationships, or managing your daily routine?

Yeah, outside work it shows up too, but it’s sort of the same pattern. I’ll have a bunch of things floating around—emails I meant to answer, stuff for a workshop, notes I was going to sort through, even little deadlines—and I don’t seem to line them up in any sensible order.

I end up grabbing whatever feels most urgent or noisy in the moment, even if it’s not actually the thing that matters most. It’s frustrating because I can see all the pieces, I just can’t seem to keep them organized long enough to move through them properly.
Can you think of specific examples from your daily life—like chores, personal projects, or even managing your schedule—where this disorganization and difficulty prioritizing has caused real problems?

Yeah, I mean… the biggest example is kind of the whole mix of things I’m juggling. I’ll have patent notes that need sorting, workshop prep that has an actual sequence to it, gallery deadlines coming up, and decisions I owe the team, and instead of laying it out in order, I just sort of… bounce to whatever is making the most noise.

Like, if an email comes in about the gallery, suddenly that feels urgent, even though maybe the workshop prep is actually the thing that will take longer. Or I’ll start reorganizing notes because they’re right in front of me, and then realize I never made the decision someone was waiting on.

It’s not that I don’t care about the priorities. I can talk through them if someone asks me. But when I’m on my own, all the moving parts kind of flatten out, and I grab the loudest one. Then I end the day with important stuff still sitting there, half-started or not started.
Can you tell me if this pattern of disorganization and difficulty prioritizing has been present since your childhood, or if it’s something that’s developed more recently?

Yeah, no, looking back, it wasn’t just recent. I think I used to tell myself it was because life got more complicated—work, projects, all that—but when I think about grade school, it was kind of there already.

Teachers would write things like I was bright, but I’d be daydreaming, or I’d forget to turn in assignments that I’d actually finished. Which is such a weirdly specific memory, because I can still remember having the paper done and then it just living in my folder like it didn’t exist. And I lost homework folders a lot too, way before I was a teenager. So… yeah, I think the pattern goes back pretty far.
When you were younger, did you have trouble staying seated, often fidgeting or feeling restless, or did you have difficulty waiting your turn or interrupting others?

Yeah… I don’t remember being the kid who was constantly jumping out of his seat, exactly. But restlessness, yes, that’s familiar.

Even now, on long design calls, I can feel this sort of pressure building in my body, like I need to move. I’ll pace around my office or switch from one chair to another while I’m trying to look like I’m fully focused. Sometimes I’ll angle the camera so it’s not obvious, which is ridiculous, but it helps me get through the call.

As a kid, I’m less clear on the “waiting my turn” or interrupting part. The physical restlessness is easier for me to recognize now than to remember clearly from back then.
Do you often find yourself losing things necessary for tasks or activities, like keys, wallets, or paperwork, even when you know you need them?

Yeah, definitely. I lose the little things I need to actually do the work all the time—USB-C adapters, my stylus, my sketchbook, my badge… and it’s not like I don’t know they’re important.

It’s more like I set them down somewhere and then there’s just no trace of that moment in my head. I’ll spend half the morning opening the same drawer three times, checking bags I already checked, getting irritated, and then I find the adapter sitting next to the coffee machine or something. And by then I’ve lost the thread of what I was supposed to be doing.

It sounds small, but it can really derail me.
Do you find that you often fail to give close attention to details or make careless mistakes in your work or other activities?

Yeah, that happens. Not usually huge dramatic mistakes, more like... embarrassingly small stuff that I somehow don’t see.

Like in code reviews, I’ll miss a reversed condition or some tiny version number in a dependency file, and then later when someone points it out, I’m staring at it thinking, “How did I not catch that?” It was right there. I think I skim past it, especially if the surrounding code looks familiar.

And then I’ll get distracted thinking about how we probably shouldn’t even have that dependency structured that way, or how the build system is kind of a mess, which is maybe not the question. But yeah—the close-detail thing, I do make those careless misses.
Have you noticed any days where you feel down or lose interest in things you usually enjoy, even for a little while?

I’m not sure. I mean, everyone has off days, right? There are days where I’m kind of flat or I don’t really want to do anything, but I don’t know that I’d call it losing interest exactly.

Sometimes I’ll avoid things I normally like just because starting them feels weirdly like too much effort, even if it’s something enjoyable. Like I’ll stare at a book or a game or whatever and then end up scrolling articles about mechanical keyboards for an hour, which is not really the same thing.

But feeling down… not in a way I’ve clearly tracked, I guess. I haven’t really noticed a pattern.
